Ok, well, I guess that's a lot. If I hadn't seen any of them, I'd start with these 5 in this order (not counting Assault on Arkham which would be #3 for me):

  • Batman: The Killing Joke
    Note: This wasn't everything I'd hoped it be. It's a great Batman movie, but being the Killing Joke story arc, I'd hoped it would be the perfect Batman movie. It wasn't, but it was pretty great regardless.
  • Justice League: The Flashpoint Paradox
    This movie covers the comic story arc that involves the Flash and an alternate timeline of the main Earth where, due to a special factor, the Justice League never formed and it's currently all-out war between the Atlantians and the Amazonians. Easily one of the most intense of the movies.
  • Justice League: Gods and Monsters
    Alternate Earth where each of the main Justice League founders has a very interesting origin story twist about them. I enjoyed it a lot also because it was done in the Batman: The Animated Series art style, so nostalgia trip.

Note: The 4th and 5th slot are the two that are hard for me to fill. The top 3 are "must watches" to me. Not counting those, the other 80% of the movies are good movies with a couple duds in there. These following two are just two I picked that I particularly enjoyed, but you can watch whatever off the list and have an enjoyable experience imo.

One dud (completely subjective of course) would be Green Lantern: Emerald Knights because although I enjoyed learning a bit of back story about the Green Lantern Corp, it wasn't very well done honestly. It felt very "follow the tropes" and there was little that was interesting about it.

Another dud would be Batman: Bad Blood for me. It was... weird. The story wasn't taken from the comics and was entirely original. It involved Batwoman (not Batgirl). She uses guns and wears a strange costume. Not exactly top tier quality for me either.

Justice League VS. Teen Titans was just "ok".

  • Justice League: War
    Covering the Justice League's main members first meeting one another, this introduces Darkseid and gives the origin story for Cyborg. It's the New 52 version of the heroes. What made this movie? Batman meeting Superman for the first time in combat. This combined with Batman: The Dark Knight Returns covers what happened in Superman V Batman essentially in a better way imo. Thus why I'm recommending these as my 4th and 5th.
  • Batman: The Dark Knight Returns
    This one covers after Bruce is like 50ish years old and hasn't been the caped crusader for a while. It covers an arc from the comics that the Superman V Batman movie covered, and imo in a better way. Think pre-Batman Beyond era. Weird villains, but I enjoyed the Batman V Superman stuff. It's occurring in an extended Cold War era btw, so that should give you a feel for what Batman/Superman this is (if Kennedy as president didn't tell you that already). I think everyone is skewed towards Marvel, honestly, because of the successful Deadpool marketing. That's it.

DC is more iconic. The stories are more epic and allegorical and tasteful.

Does everyone forget that the plan has been to brighten the colour palette from Man of Steel forward? A world before superheroes is dark. Superman brings colour and slowly the world gets more bright.

Wild speculation now: The Flash, in a fanboy moment of wanting to impress Bruce Wayne, goes back in time to stop Superman from killing General Zod, causing the cinematic Flashpoint Paradox.

I don't think the skew towards Marvel is just because of Deadpool. If Marvel hadn't been cranking out good movies or watchable leads, there is not a snowball's chance in hell Deadpool would ever have been made. Indeed Ryan Reynolds and his co-conspirators had to more or less beg the studio bosses for enough money to make the film. Deadpool's ROI is only massive because of its piddling budget: it made $745 million worldwide, on a budget of $58 million. I can't think of the last big superhero film that was made for less than a hundred million "official". Shit, they even joke about how cheap the studio was in the film itself.

Part of the reason I suspect they kept the purse strings tied down so tight was because Deadpool with an 'R' rating was an enormous risk for a studio to take: nobody had made a seriously violent superhero film before (unless you count Watchmen or maybe The Punisher, and they largely tanked.) Deadpool is lightning in a bottle in the sense that the script dares to fourth-wall pretty much the entire superhero genre, and for once it's actually laugh-out-loud funny in parts. Whether they can pull off the same trick twice is another thing entirely, and I suspect Deadpool's thing is going to get old a lot faster than the makers think it will.

Point being: Deadpool's performance is more of an outlier than a rule for Marvel. If there's a single cause for Marvel's success with its films, I think it comes down to Robert Downey Jr's performance in the first Iron Man film. If he hadn't crushed it completely, there would never have been a second Iron Man film and probably no Avengers. The fact they keep wheeling him out past the end of his character's arc proves how integral he is to the franchise ... although I think they underestimated how much heart Chris Evans as Captain America has, too.

I'm not really sure about the idea that the colour palette of DC films is getting much brighter. Justice League has all the hue and saturation of a Bogart noir film given what we've seen of it thus far. Unfortunately, while it's a bit shit to place all the blame at one door, for me it comes down to the fact Zack Snyder is running the joint. David Ayers directed SS, but Snyder executive produced it, meaning Snyder's hand is still firmly in how the film looks and plays. Man of Steel I thought succeeded because Snyder had Nolan around to restrain him, but since then Snyder's fallen firmly back into his comfortable groove, which is, in essence, directing full-length feature films with all the sensibility and attention span of a director of music videos. Snyder keeps directing comic book films looking for specific images or moments, and it just does not fucking work: a motion picture is not the same medium as a comic book, and a comic book is not a set of storyboards for a completed film.

I agree DC is more iconic. Someone once said the fundamental difference between Marvel and DC is that Marvel's characters are basically soap opera characters: everything rests on new plot twists and new shit happening to these guys. DC's characters are more illustrations of concepts: Superman represents truth, justice, and the American way, Batman represents justice unblinded, Wonder Woman represents armed peace. It's tougher therefore to write scripts for these guys, but it's foolish for DC to try and play on Marvel's turf and try and make the characters themselves soap opera types like Wolverine or Iron Man. Suicide Squad was an attempt at the latter I guess.
